benchmark_vs_tool_note: Both papers are benchmarks, not tools. What can count toward a construct: (a) CORE-Bench's baseline CORE-Agent (AutoGPT variant) which takes a code capsule + task prompt, installs deps, runs code, and emits report.json of extracted result values; (b) PaperBench's BasicAgent/IterativeAgent which takes only the paper (author code is blacklisted) and emits a from-scratch repo + reproduce.sh + README.md; (c) PaperBench's author-co-developed hierarchical rubrics + addendums, and its SimpleJudge which grades each rubric leaf against submission files with a 0/1 score plus explanation. Neither benchmark's construction pipeline (paper selection, task-question writing) is a user-facing deliverable.

UC1.evidence: please also include a README.md file that describes what you were able to achieve in your reproduction attempt, explains how your codebase relates to various parts of the reproduction (PaperBench App. F.3, Fig. 13, p.29)
UC1.note: Debatable: PaperBench requires the agent to write a README (artifact description, code-to-claims map, expected outcomes) but it documents the agent's own generated artifact, is not venue-format, and is not evaluated as a deliverable; CORE-Bench has nothing.

UC3.evidence: Explore the files provided for the submission along with the output logs to identify the parts that are relevant to the resolution criteria ... be explicit about which files you are referring to (PaperBench Fig. 9, p.27)
UC3.note: PaperBench's judge maps each rubric leaf (a paper claim/result/method requirement) to specific submission files and logs as an internal grading step, and the required README must explain 'how your codebase relates to various parts of the reproduction'; CORE-Bench's task questions link figures/tables to result files but are hand-built and the agent only returns values.

UC4.evidence: If either 'reproduce.sh' or 'reproduce.log' is missing, you should consider any criteria relying on it to have failed. (PaperBench Fig. 8, p.26)
UC4.note: Debatable: PaperBench's judge reports per-requirement failures with explanations, but the reference is a paper-specific replication rubric, not a packaging/venue standard; the only standard-like checks are reproduce.sh/README presence and the 1GB limit.

UC5.evidence: We manually create an addendum for each paper containing clarifications from the paper's original authors. The addendums also clarify when parts of the paper are out of scope. (PaperBench Sec. 3.2, p.6)
UC5.note: Partial only by the rubric's letter: PaperBench documents paper underspecification (addendums, App. B gpt-4o 'Reproducibility Filter' requiring 'sufficient detail'), and footnote 8 observes author codebases 'are often incomplete or contain bugs' when judged; but this is manual benchmark construction, not agent/judge output. CORE-Bench explicitly excludes checking paper claims: 'not to ensure that the results reported directly in the paper are correct' (Sec. 2.1, p.6).

UC6.evidence: The candidate must produce a submission which consists of a repository including all the code required to reproduce the paper's empirical results. This repository must include a reproduce.sh file at its root (PaperBench Sec. 2.1, p.2)
UC6.note: PaperBench's whole task is generating code + environment/run script + README from P alone (author code blacklisted); a strict reading of the rubric's 'ML papers only' example would drop this to 1 since it is validated only on 20 ICML papers. CORE-Bench-Hard generates dependency installs/run commands but from A (README), never from P.

UC8.note: PaperBench Sec. 6 relates itself to CORE-Bench in prose, but neither benchmark links papers to each other as a task.

B1.evidence: authors could verify their work's reproducibility before publication, independent researchers could more easily replicate past studies, and conference organizers and journal editors could efficiently assess the reproducibility of submissions (CORE-Bench Sec. 1, p.4)
B1.note: Primary users are AI-agent developers/evaluators, so n/a is defensible; if forced, CORE-Bench names both authors and editors (~3) and PaperBench's judge is evaluator-facing (~4-5).

B2.evidence: we copy its submission to a fresh VM running an Ubuntu 24.04 image with access to an A10 GPU. We execute the submission's reproduction script to generate results from a clean start. (PaperBench Sec. 2.2, p.3)
B2.note: CORE-Bench-Medium/Hard agents must run Docker or install deps and execute code (Table 3, p.6); only PaperBench Code-Dev and CORE-Bench-Easy skip execution.

B3.evidence: CORE-Bench (Siegel et al., 2024) tasks agents to reproduce the results of a research paper given its repository. In contrast, PaperBench tasks agents to replicate the results of a research paper from scratch. (PaperBench Sec. 6, p.9)
B3.note: Bimodal, not 4: CORE-Bench is 5 (agent gets capsule/README/Dockerfile and never the paper), PaperBench is 1 (agent gets only paper PDF/markdown + addendum; author code blacklisted); the judge reads paper + submission (~3).

B4.evidence: Each paper is accompanied by a manually created rubric, which specifies all the necessary outcomes for replicating the paper in detail; resulting in a total of 8,316 individually gradable outcomes (PaperBench Sec. 1, p.1)
B4.note: Split: CORE-Bench is ~1 (success = values within a 95% prediction interval of manual runs, Fig. 4, p.7; no external standard); PaperBench is ~4 (grading is driven entirely by explicit, published, author-approved rubrics plus submission rules), though the rubrics are per-paper criteria, not a venue standard.

B5.evidence: We report task accuracy as the main metric, which is the proportion of tasks for which all of the task questions have been answered correctly. (CORE-Bench Sec. 3, p.9)
B5.note: PaperBench likewise emits a Replication Score (Sec. 2.3, p.3) with per-leaf 0/1 plus short explanation; the agent-side README is prose but the benchmark's output is a score.

disagreements: UC3: current 0, should be 1 because PaperBench's SimpleJudge maps every rubric leaf (derived from paper claims/results) to specific submission files/logs as an internal grading step, and the task requires a README explaining how the codebase relates to parts of the reproduction (Fig. 9 p.27; Fig. 13 p.29).

UC5: current 0, arguably 1 (low confidence) because PaperBench documents paper underspecification via author addendums and a gpt-4o 'sufficient detail' reproducibility filter (Sec. 3.2 p.6; App. B p.13), and judging author codebases exposes paper-artifact gaps (fn. 8 p.6); all of this is manual benchmark construction, so 0 remains defensible.

UC6: current 0, should be 2 because PaperBench's central task is generating a full artifact (code, reproduce.sh environment script, README) from the paper alone with author code blacklisted (Sec. 2.1 p.2; Fig. 13 p.29); 1 if the rubric's 'ML papers only' subclass rule is applied strictly. CORE-Bench contributes nothing here (starts from A).

B3: current 4, should be 3 (or split CORE=5 / PaperBench=1) because PaperBench agents receive only the paper and are forbidden the artifact, while CORE-Bench agents receive only the artifact and never the paper (PaperBench Sec. 6 p.9; CORE Table 3 p.6).

B4: current 1, should be 3 (or split CORE=1 / PaperBench=4) because PaperBench grading is driven by explicit, published, author-approved rubrics with 8,316 gradable criteria plus submission rules (Sec. 1 p.1; Sec. 3.1 p.5), whereas CORE-Bench is standard-agnostic.
one_line_summary: Two agent benchmarks: CORE-Bench scores agents on re-running a given repo to extract results; PaperBench scores agents on rebuilding an ML paper's artifact from the paper alone, judged by author-approved rubrics.
